report.message:
The symptoms match past incidents where a region-wide front-end failure in an object store made all object APIs fail and cascaded to dependent products.

### Region-wide front-end configuration change exposing a latent bug (confidence: medium)
**What happened:** In DAN-044, a configuration change to the Azure Storage Blob Front-Ends exposed a bug that put the front ends into an infinite loop, so they could not take traffic. This matches your case: all object APIs (read, enumerate, write, erase) are failing across an entire region, with the same cascade to VM provisioning, disk volumes, functions and the control panel. The current report does not mention a configuration change, and DAN-044 does not describe status page controls being unable to post product-specific notices.

**How it was fixed:**
- Roll back the configuration change.
- Restart the storage front ends.

**How to prevent it:**
- Apply production changes in incremental batches rather than across most regions in a short period.
- Improve processes to ensure such incidents do not recur.

**Source:** [Update on Azure Storage Service Interruption | Microsoft Azure Blog](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/blog/update-on-azure-storage-service-interruption/)

### Routine scaling event crossing a capacity threshold (confidence: medium)
**What happened:** In DAN-114, the Lambda Frontend fleet scaled with normal traffic growth and crossed a capacity threshold never reached before, triggering a latent defect that left front ends unable to serve requests and cascading to dependent services. In DAN-110, scaling the Kinesis front-end cache fleet caused servers to exceed an operating-system thread limit, leaving front ends unable to route requests. This matches your region-wide front-end/API failure pattern and cascade to VMs, functions and the management console. The current report mentions no traffic growth or scaling trigger, and the affected service is an object store rather than Lambda or Kinesis.

**How it was fixed:**
- Scale down the front-end fleet to a level that no longer triggers the defect.
- Remove the additional capacity that triggered the event.
- Restart the front-end servers.

**How to prevent it:**
- Disable the scaling activities that triggered the event while the latent bug is fixed.
- Move to larger CPU and memory servers, reducing the total number of servers and threads required.
- Add fine-grained alarming for thread consumption.
- Test an increase in thread count limits in the operating system configuration.
- Make changes to improve the cold-start time for the front-end fleet.
- Move the front-end server cache to a dedicated fleet.
- Bound cells to a well-tested size to avoid unexpected scaling issues.

**Source:** [Summary of the AWS Service Event in the Northern Virginia (US-EAST-1) Region](https://aws.amazon.com/message/061323/)
**Source:** [Summary of the Amazon Kinesis Event in the Northern Virginia (US-EAST-1) Region](https://aws.amazon.com/message/11201/)

### Other possibility: Latent memory-leak or resource-exhaustion bug in storage server agent (confidence: low)
A latent memory leak in a reporting agent on EBS storage servers consumed memory until servers could no longer process customer requests, as in DAN-107. Your case differs: there is no mention of a data-collection server failure, DNS change, or memory-pressure symptom, and the failure is across all front-end API operations rather than only stuck volumes. **Source:** [Summary of the October 22, 2012 AWS Service Event in the US-East Region](https://aws.amazon.com/message/680342/)

- Whether a configuration change was rolled out to the object store front-end fleet before the failure.
- Whether a scaling event or traffic growth occurred before the failure.
- Error messages or logs showing whether requests are timing out, looping, or being rejected.
- Whether the failing component is the object store front ends or the storage servers.
- Whether the status page control failure is a separate dependency issue or part of the same outage.

report.message:
The symptoms most closely match a past incident in which a Redis primary node failed or was migrated, causing a cluster rebalance and cascading failures through API workers, hosting workers, and session workers.

### Redis primary failover or migration (confidence: high)
**What happened:** In the past incident, a Redis instance acting as the primary for a highly available cluster used by API services was migrated automatically, causing the node to drop offline and forcing the cluster to rebalance. API instances did not handle the Redis failover correctly, which degraded the API service and cascaded into a full real-time system failure. It matches your case: API workers struggling to connect to Redis, slow calls, clients struggling to join, hosting workers acting strangely, and session workers behaving abnormally.

**How it was fixed:**
- Rolling restart of all API instances to resolve Redis connection issues.
- Corrected an improperly cached route so it handles this type of error properly without degrading other services.
- Added monitoring around signals that would alert engineers to a cascading failure early.

**How to prevent it:**
- Increase the priority of fixing known issues with Redis failovers.
- Add monitoring around signals that would alert to a cascading failure with enough time to investigate and prepare.
- Continue planning to improve the overall reliability and failure handling of the affected services.

**Source:** [Discord Status - Unavailable Guilds & Connection Issues](https://status.discordapp.com/incidents/qk9cdgnqnhcn)

### Cache-node removal or capacity reduction (confidence: medium)
**What happened:** In the past incident, cache nodes were removed sequentially from the fleet, causing the cache hit rate to drop. The application then had to run queries on every shard, overwhelming the database and triggering a cascading failure. It matches your case: slow calls, failed connections, clients struggling to join, and a cascading failure in a messaging application. It differs because the current incident mentions no Consul update or cache-node removal, and there is no mention of Vitess scatter queries or channel membership tables.

**How it was fixed:**
- Paused the Consul agent restart operation that had triggered the problem.
- Modified the problematic scatter query to read from a table sharded by channel.
- Analyzed other database queries fronted by the caching tier to find other high-volume scatter queries.
- Made changes to the process for performing Consul rollouts to avoid triggering this failure mode again during upgrades.

**How to prevent it:**
- Changes to the process for performing Consul rollouts so this failure mode is not triggered again during upgrades.
- Explore other ways of increasing the resilience of the caching tier.

**Source:** [Slack’s Incident on 2-22-22 | Engineering at Slack](https://slack.engineering/slacks-incident-on-2-22-22/)

### Other possibility: Routine maintenance or automation malfunction (confidence: low)
A routine maintenance or automation malfunction once corrupted code on workers, disconnecting users; the resulting mass simultaneous reconnections overwhelmed the database and caused cascading connection failures. Your case shares the messaging service kind and symptoms such as workers acting strangely and clients struggling to join, but it centers on Redis connection struggles and mentions no automation malfunction or code deploy. **Source:** [This was not normal. Really. | The Official Slack Blog](https://web.archive.org/web/20181208123409/https://slackhq.com/this-was-not-normal-really)

**What to check now**
- Whether a Redis primary node failed or was migrated recently.
- Whether API workers' Redis connection errors are timeouts, authentication failures, or failover handling bugs.
- Whether the costly API operation being hammered is a client reconnection or join endpoint.
- What "acting strangely" means for the hosting and session workers (crashes, OOM, loop, etc.).
- Whether any change, deploy, or maintenance occurred just before the failure.

report.message:
The symptoms match a past Consul outage: slow KV writes, Raft leader/peer desynchronization, elevated CPU, and downstream health-check failures.

### Consul streaming feature rollout causing BoltDB snapshot pressure (confidence: medium)
**What happened:** In the past incident, enabling a Consul streaming feature increased load on the service-discovery cluster, causing BoltDB snapshot pressure, slow KV writes, Raft leader/peer desynchronization, elevated CPU on one host, and downstream health-check failures. It matches your case: the same component kind (Consul service-discovery cluster with Raft voting peers and BoltDB KV store) and very similar symptoms.

**How it was fixed:**
- Disabled the streaming feature for all Consul systems, including the traffic routing nodes.

**How to prevent it:**
- Remove the circular dependency between telemetry systems and Consul.
- Extend telemetry systems to provide better visibility into Consul and BoltDB performance.
- Add highly targeted alerts if there are any signs that the system is approaching the state that caused the outage.
- Extend telemetry systems to provide more visibility into the traffic patterns between services and Consul.

**Source:** [Roblox - Roblox Return to Service  | Roblox](https://blog.roblox.com/2022/01/roblox-return-to-service-10-28-10-31-2021/)

### BoltDB file growth from un-reclaimed free pages after repeated snapshots (confidence: medium)
**What happened:** In the past incident, BoltDB file growth from un-reclaimed free pages after repeated snapshots degraded write performance and Raft replication on the Consul cluster, leading to slow KV updates, leader desynchronization, and downstream failures. It matches your case: same component kind (Consul with BoltDB persistence) and matching symptoms (slow KV writes, members falling behind, primary losing sync with voting peers, elevated CPU on a single host).

**How it was fixed:**
- Disabled the streaming feature for all Consul systems, including the traffic routing nodes.

**How to prevent it:**

**Source:** [Roblox - Roblox Return to Service  | Roblox](https://blog.roblox.com/2022/01/roblox-return-to-service-10-28-10-31-2021/)

### Other possibility: Primary node failure or migration triggering a rebalance (confidence: low)
A primary node failure or migration in a Redis cluster once triggered a rebalance that downstream applications could not handle, causing cascading health-check failures. Your case involves Consul/BoltDB service discovery with no mention of a node migration or failover, and the symptoms center on slow KV writes and Raft sync rather than cache misconfiguration. **Source:** [Discord - Discord Status - Unavailable Guilds & Connection Issues](https://status.discordapp.com/incidents/qk9cdgnqnhcn)

- Whether the affected cluster is Consul, whether BoltDB is the storage backend, and whether snapshots are enabled and growing.
- Which host has elevated CPU, whether it is the Raft leader, and whether leader elections are occurring.
- Error messages or logs from the service-discovery cluster and downstream applications.

report.message:
The symptoms point to database CPU exhaustion taking the CI browser side offline while background jobs kept running.

### Database CPU exhaustion under load (confidence: medium)
**What happened:** The database ran out of CPU capacity under load, so web servers could not open connections; health checks failed, the load balancer removed unhealthy hosts, and new hosts never passed their checks, taking the CI browser side offline while background jobs kept running. This matches your case: database CPU is exhausted, web probes cannot connect to the database, and the traffic distributor is cycling machines out of rotation. The difference is that the past incidents had a known trigger (a database downgrade, recent changes, or a mass reconnection event), while no trigger is mentioned for your incident.

**How it was fixed:**
- Roll back recent changes.
- Fail over to a different primary to kill queued operations.
- Bring up excess capacity to handle the backlog.
- Add new metrics to debug the problem.
- Update throttling code to improve behavior.
- Move data onto its own deployment and build out a new DB cluster.
- Upgrade the database to an instance type that can handle the load.
- Roll out new servers.
- Remove the centralized pgbouncer server and revert to pgbouncer installed on each host.
- Add additional database capacity.
- Make optimizations to reconnection methods to reduce total capacity needed.

**How to prevent it:**
- Rebuild the queue model to take strain off the database.
- Add tools to deal with similar situations.
- Load test after significant infrastructure changes.
- Stop health checks and autoscaling rules when seeing high churn issues in AWS.
- Change Auto Scaling Groups to EC2 health checks and lock in desired counts.
- Suspend and resume Auto Scaling Processes.
- Make changes to Pacemaker configuration so failover of the active database role only occurs when initiated by a member of the operations team.
- Investigate solutions to ensure failovers do not impact performance.
- Perform a full audit of the Pacemaker and Heartbeat stack.

- Modify the behavior of improperly cached routes to handle errors without degrading other services.
- Increase the priority of fixing known Redis failover issues.
- Fix the faulty retry behavior in the client.
- Add rate limiting for log messages.

### Service token client secrets overwritten (confidence: medium)
**What happened:** In DAN-009, a code release that manages service tokens overwrote client secret values with empty strings, so every request authenticated with a service token failed. This matches your incident: authorization failures on a key-based data store cascade to hosted websites, sign-in, edge workload publishing, and release reversal tools. The difference is that your report does not mention a code release just before the failure, and the affected store is described generically rather than explicitly as R2.

**How it was fixed:**
- Manually restore the correct service token values for the accounts with overwritten service tokens.
- Restore the service tokens of all impacted accounts from an older database copy.

**How to prevent it:**
- Add unit tests that automatically catch similar issues with service token overwrites before new features are launched.
- Implement an automatic alert for any dramatic increase in failed service token authentication requests.
- Make process improvements to allow faster rollbacks for specific database tables.
- Update all relevant database fields to include checks for empty strings on top of existing "not null checks".

**Source:** [Cloudflare incident on January 24, 2023 | Cloudflare Blog](https://blog.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-incident-on-january-24th-2023/)

### Database schema limit on token table (confidence: medium)
**What happened:** In DAN-095, a foreign key on the scoped-tokens table reached max INT32, causing high failure rates for Actions and Pages and breaking scoped-token Git operations. This matches your incident in that a database/token table underpinning authorization failed and cascaded to dependent products such as websites, sign-in, and edge publishing. The difference is that DAN-095 was an integer overflow on a scoped-tokens table, not a global authorization rejection of all reads, writes, removals, and enumerations on a key-value store, and no trigger is mentioned in your incident.

**How it was fixed:**
- Perform a long-running schema migration to INT64.

**How to prevent it:**
- Manually audit all INT32 columns.
- Investigate further improvements to automation to help prevent these types of issues.

**Source:** [GitHub Availability Report: May 2021 - The GitHub Blog](https://github.blog/news-insights/company-news/github-availability-report-may-2021/)

A telemetry gap once caused security policies to be auto-applied to backend storage accounts, blocking access and taking down dependent products worldwide, but your incident reports no telemetry or security-policy change and the failure pattern is a direct authorization rejection on every read/write/removal/enumeration rather than blocked VM metadata and compute operations. **Source:** [GitHub availability report: February 2026 - The GitHub Blog](https://github.blog/news-insights/company-news/github-availability-report-february-2026/)

- Error messages or logs showing whether failures are authentication (token/secret) versus authorization (policy) errors.

report.message:
The symptoms match two past Postgres incidents. The strongest match is a WAL-retention problem on the primary that broke replication and made recovery fail; a secondary possibility is a bad configuration change that prevented the database from starting.

### WAL segments removed before the replica could replicate them (confidence: high)
**What happened:** In the past incident, a load spike caused the primary to remove WAL segments before the secondary could replicate them, so replication stopped. Fresh `pg_basebackup` attempts hung or failed because the primary did not have enough replication connections (`max_wal_senders`). When engineers temporarily raised `max_wal_senders` from 3 to 32, PostgreSQL refused to restart because too many semaphores were being created. This matches your case: replica synchronization ceased because WAL segments were no longer on the main server, base-copy attempts stalled, a replication-slot shortage was reported, and after a configuration change the database failed to start due to excessive semaphore allocation.

**How it was fixed:**
- Temporarily increased `max_wal_senders` from 3 to 32.
- Wiped the secondary data directory and ran `pg_basebackup` to re-synchronize manually.

**How to prevent it:**
- Set PostgreSQL's `max_connections` to a sane value.
- Investigate point-in-time recovery and continuous archiving for PostgreSQL.
- Take hourly LVM snapshots of production databases.
- Take Azure disk snapshots of production databases.
- Move staging to the ARM environment.
- Recover production replicas.
- Automate testing of recovering PostgreSQL database backups.
- Improve PostgreSQL replication documentation and runbooks.
- Investigate pgbarman for creating PostgreSQL backups.
- Investigate using WAL-E for database backup and realtime replication.
- Build streaming database restore.
- Assign an owner for data durability.
- Set up a public backup monitoring dashboard.

**Source:** [Gitlab - Postmortem of database outage of January 31](https://about.gitlab.com/2017/02/10/postmortem-of-database-outage-of-january-31/)

### Other possibility: Bad configuration change made the database cluster unable to start (confidence: medium)
A bad configuration change combined with other failures took a database cluster offline and required manual intervention, as in the GoCardless incident. Your case also involves a configuration change and a database that failed to start, but the GoCardless incident was caused by a disk array failure and Pacemaker misconfiguration, not WAL segment removal or semaphore exhaustion. **Source:** [GoCardless - Incident review: API and Dashboard outage on 10 October 2017 | GoCardless](https://gocardless.com/blog/incident-review-api-and-dashboard-outage-on-10th-october/)

**What to check now**
- The exact configuration change made right before the failure.
- Whether WAL archiving was enabled and whether WAL segments were removed from the primary.
- Which Postgres parameter caused the 'excessive semaphore allocation' startup error.
- Whether the replication slot shortage was a cause or a symptom of the failed base-copy attempts.

report.message:
The symptoms point to a WAF or edge-layer change blocking legitimate API traffic, similar to past incidents.

### WAF rule changed outside the normal pipeline (confidence: medium)
**What happened:** In DAN-004, a WAF rule was changed outside the standard Terraform pipeline and began blocking legitimate traffic to API and frontend distributions, causing CORS errors, dashboard and build failures, and fewer GitHub webhooks. This matches your case: page/dashboard won't load, build jobs won't launch, API requests fail with cross-origin errors, and fewer repository callbacks are arriving.

**How it was fixed:**
- Revert the problematic WAF rule from the affected distributions.
- Confirm error rates decrease and traffic is routed properly again.

**How to prevent it:**
- Implement stricter IAM policies that prevent direct modification of infrastructure managed by the infrastructure-as-code pipeline.
- Enhance Terraform drift detection to provide faster alerts when critical infrastructure components deviate from their expected state.
- Add technical guardrails to ensure all configuration management follows the infrastructure-as-code approach.
- Establish better protocols for implementing and testing WAF rules before they reach production.
- Add monitoring specifically for WAF behavior and traffic patterns.

**Source:** [Post Incident Report: April 4, 2025 - CircleCI UI Loading & build triggering issues](https://discuss.circleci.com/t/post-incident-report-april-4-2025-circleci-ui-loading-build-triggering-issues/53208)

### Globally propagated WAF or body-parsing configuration change hitting a code defect (confidence: medium)
**What happened:** In DAN-012, a configuration change to disable an internal WAF testing tool propagated globally without a gradual rollout, triggering a Lua exception in the proxy's rulesets module and causing HTTP 500 errors. This matches the edge/WAF component kind and a global configuration change, but differs because your case reports cross-origin/CORS problems in browsers rather than HTTP 500s, and DAN-012 does not describe fewer repository callbacks.

**How it was fixed:**
- Revert the change.

**How to prevent it:**
- Apply enhanced rollouts and versioning so data used for rapid threat response and general configuration has health validation and quick rollback capabilities.
- Streamline break glass capabilities for critical operations.
- Replace incorrectly applied hard-fail logic across critical data-plane components with fail-open error handling.

**Source:** [Cloudflare outage on December 5, 2025 | Cloudflare Blog](https://blog.cloudflare.com/5-december-2025-outage/)

### Other possibility: Poorly written WAF regular expression causing CPU exhaustion (confidence: low)
A poorly written WAF regular expression caused CPU exhaustion at the edge, taking down API and dashboard traffic globally, but it produced 502 errors and traffic drops, not browser cross-origin/CORS errors or a drop in repository callbacks. **Source:** [Details of the Cloudflare outage on July 2, 2019](https://web.archive.org/web/20211006055154/https://blog.cloudflare.com/details-of-the-cloudflare-outage-on-july-2-2019/)

**What to check now**
- Whether any WAF rule was modified, by whom, and through which pipeline.
- Whether the cross-origin errors are browser CORS preflight rejections or WAF blocks being misreported by the browser.
- Whether the repository host is sending fewer callbacks because the API is rejecting them or because the host itself is throttling.
- Error codes, WAF logs, and recent deploy details.

report.message:
The symptoms match past incidents where cache hosts went offline, media description lookups missed the cache, and the resulting database overload broke application-tier calls and playback.

### Cache hosts removed or went offline (confidence: medium)
**What happened:** Cache nodes were removed or went offline, causing media description lookups to miss the cache and hit the backend database directly. The resulting database overload made application-tier calls fail and broke playback for clients without local copies. This matches your case: cache hosts are down, the database is under pressure, media description calls are failing at the application tier, and clients with local copies can still deliver limited material.

**How it was fixed:**
- Reduced traffic to the datastores via the client boot throttle.
- Modified the inefficient query to read from Vitess only the data missing from memcached, rather than reading from every shard on each miss.
- Updated the query to read from replicas as well as Vitess primaries.
- Slowly increased the client boot rate limit back to normal traffic levels while maximizing database goodput.

**How to prevent it:**
- Roll out changes to the control loop to avoid this kind of failure.
- Analyze other database queries fronted by the caching tier for high-volume scatter queries.
- Explore other ways of increasing the resilience of the caching tier.
- Make changes in the process for performing Consul rollouts so this failure mode is not triggered again during upgrades.

**Source:** [Slack’s Incident on 2-22-22 | Engineering at Slack](https://slack.engineering/slacks-incident-on-2-22-22/)

**Source:** [BBC Online outage on Saturday 19th July 2014](https://www.bbc.co.uk/blogs/internet/entries/a37b0470-47d4-3991-82bb-a7d5b8803771)

**What happened:** A Redis or memcached cache node failed and the media API tier did not handle the failover correctly, so the failure cascaded from the cache tier to the application tier and overloaded the database. This matches your pattern of cache hosts down plus backend/media description calls failing. It differs because the past incident was triggered by an automatic cloud migration of a Redis primary, which your incident does not mention.

**Source:** [Discord - Discord Status - Unavailable Guilds & Connection Issues](https://status.discordapp.com/incidents/qk9cdgnqnhcn)

A configuration change meant to reduce metadata storage load overloaded a key lookup component, causing a cascading failure that brought down media description services and dependent web features. Your incident reports no such change, and the past incident centered on blob storage lookup rather than a media description cache/database tier. **Source:** [Google Cloud Status Dashboard — A configuration change intended to address an uptick in demand for metadata storage, which overloaded part of the...](https://status.cloud.google.com/incident/storage/19002)

- What triggered the cache hosts to go offline (deployment, automated scaling event, or independent failure).
- Whether the database pressure is the root cause or a secondary effect of cache misses.
- Which cache technology is involved (Redis, memcached, or another) and whether the media backend has a known failover bug.
- The exact error messages from failing media description calls.

### Latent software bug triggered by a configuration change (confidence: medium)
**What happened:** In DAN-154, an undiscovered bug in the edge software was triggered by a valid customer configuration change, causing 85% of the network to return errors. This matches your case: widespread edge errors worldwide from a similar component and symptom pattern. It differs because the current analyst mentions no change at all.

**How it was fixed:**
- Deploy the bug fix across the network as quickly and safely as possible.
- Conduct a complete post mortem of the processes and practices followed during the incident.
- Evaluate ways to improve remediation time.

**How to prevent it:**
- Figure out why the bug was not detected during software quality assurance and testing processes.
- Continue to innovate and invest in fundamental changes to the safety of the underlying platforms.

**Source:** [Summary of June 8 outage | Fastly](https://www.fastly.com/blog/summary-of-june-8-outage)

### Poorly written WAF regular expression causing CPU exhaustion (confidence: medium)
**What happened:** In DAN-137, a single WAF rule with a poorly written regular expression caused excessive backtracking and CPU exhaustion, leading to global downtime and widespread 502 errors. This matches your case: same edge/CDN component and worldwide symptom pattern. It differs because the current analyst reports no WAF rule deployment before the problem.

**How it was fixed:**
- Stop all release work on the WAF.
- Re-introduce the excessive CPU usage protection that got removed.
- Manually inspect all WAF Managed Rules to find and correct other instances of possible excessive backtracking.
- Introduce performance profiling for all rules to the test suite.
- Switch to either the re2 or Rust regex engine which both have run-time guarantees.
- Change the SOP to do staged rollouts of rules.
- Put in place an emergency ability to take the Cloudflare Dashboard and API off Cloudflare's edge.
- Automate update of the Cloudflare Status page.

**How to prevent it:**
- Port the WAF to use the new firewall engine.

**Source:** [Details of the Cloudflare outage on July 2, 2019](https://web.archive.org/web/20211006055154/https://blog.cloudflare.com/details-of-the-cloudflare-outage-on-july-2-2019/)

**What happened:** In DAN-005, an operations team added a packet-drop rule to edge routers via Flowspec, causing routers to consume all their RAM and crash, taking down the edge network worldwide. This matches your case: same edge router component and worldwide symptom pattern. It differs because the current analyst mentions no change and there is no mention of routers or Flowspec.

**How it was fixed:**
- Remove the bad rule.
- Call network operations teams in the data centers where routers were unresponsive to physically access the routers and perform a hard reboot.

**How to prevent it:**
- Put more controls in place to eliminate problems like this in the future.

**Source:** [Today's Outage Post Mortem](https://web.archive.org/web/20211006135542/https://blog.cloudflare.com/todays-outage-post-mortem-82515/)

- Whether any configuration change, rule deployment, or software deployment preceded the errors.
- Which specific edge component is failing (WAF, edge routers, origin fetch layer, TLS termination, etc.).
- What error codes are being returned (HTTP 5xx, connection timeouts, DNS failures, or something else).

report.message:
No past incident matches your situation, so I cannot identify a confirmed cause.

**What is missing:**
- No past incident describes a hosted database provisioning API rejecting a parameter without a known change.
- It is unknown whether the sporadic rejections are caused by a regional rollout, a flaky dependency, or intermittent validation logic.
- The diagnostic does not say which parameter caused the rejection, so the failing component cannot be confirmed.

**What to check now**
- Check whether the provider made any unannounced change to the provisioning API or its validation rules.
- Check whether the rejections correlate with a specific region (US East was hit first) or with a specific parameter value.
- Check whether the rejection happens only for certain parameter combinations or at certain times.
- Look for provider-side change logs or status updates around the time the first rejection appeared in the early evening UTC.
